clinical_knowledge.topic: Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (Concussion) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (Concussion) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (Concussion), ruling out intracranial hemorrhage, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: throbbing headache, dizziness, and mild nausea after bumping head in basketball

Key HPI features: 20M college student presents 4 hours after colliding with another player during basketball and bumping his head. Experienced brief disorientation but no loss of consciousness. Complains of mild headache and dizziness.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (Concussion), ruling out intracranial hemorrhage.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (Concussion).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Intracranial hemorrhage without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Worsening headache, repeated vomiting, or increasing confusion — would suggest a more serious brain injury.
management_principles: Perform a neurological and balance exam to evaluate for Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (Concussion), ruling out intracranial hemorrhage
Apply the Canadian CT Head Rule only after confirming eligibility and assessing all high- and medium-risk features, anticoagulant use, and neurologic examination
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: throbbing headache, dizziness, and mild nausea after bumping head in basketball

20M college student presents 4 hours after colliding with another player during basketball and bumping his head. Experienced brief disorientation but no loss of consciousness. Complains of mild headache and dizziness.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination. Evaluate for pertinent signs.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (Concussion), ruling out intracranial hemorrhage.
reference_soap.plan: Perform a complete neurologic examination and assess for anticoagulant use. Apply the Canadian CT Head Rule only after confirming eligibility and assessing all high- and medium-risk features; obtain CT if indicated. If discharged, provide written return precautions for worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, increasing confusion, weakness, or drowsiness. Recommend 24-48 hours of relative rest followed by graded return to school/work and sport only after symptom resolution and supervised progression.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (Concussion), ruling out intracranial hemorrhage.
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for throbbing headache, dizziness, and mild nausea after bumping head in basketball
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for emergency medicine
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (Concussion), ruling out intracranial hemorrhage.

teaching.one_liner: A blow to the head causing transient neurological disturbance — brief disorientation, headache, dizziness — without loss of consciousness; the Canadian CT Head Rule determines whether imaging is needed.
red_flags: Worsening headache, repeated vomiting, or increasing confusion — would suggest a more serious brain injury

must_ask.say: Did you lose consciousness, even briefly?
Do you remember exactly what happened during and right after the collision?
How is your headache and dizziness right now?
Have you vomited since the injury?
Have you had a concussion before?

history.answer: I bumped my head during a basketball game about four hours ago, and now I have a throbbing headache and feel dizzy.
The headache started right after the hit and built up over fifteen to twenty minutes rather than peaking instantly.
It has been a continuous ache for the past four hours, staying about the same without suddenly getting worse.
It throbs across my forehead and on the right temple area where I collided with the other player.
It feels like a dull, throbbing pressure, around a 4 out of 10 in severity.
Quick head turns and bright screens make it worse, while resting quietly in a dark room makes it feel a bit better.
No, I didn't see any flashing lights, blind spots, or wavy lines before or after the hit.
I feel mildly nauseous and uneasy in my stomach, but I haven't thrown up at all.
Yes, bright fluorescent lights and loud noises definitely make my headache worse.
No, my eyes aren't watering or red, and I don't have a runny nose or drooping eyelids.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, neck stiffness, or rash.
I have not had any limb weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, or seizures.
My vision is clear, with no blurriness, double vision, or eye pain.
I went up for a rebound during a pickup basketball game and collided hard forehead-to-forehead with another player.
I did not pass out or lose consciousness, but I felt dazed and groggy for a few seconds right after the hit.
I remember the entire play and walking off the court to the bench without any gaps in my memory.
I feel slightly unsteady and lightheaded when I stand up or walk, but the room is not spinning.
I haven't taken any Tylenol, ibuprofen, or other pain relievers because I wanted to be evaluated first.
The only trigger was the head collision during basketball; I slept well last night and hadn't been under unusual stress.
I do not have high blood pressure, and I do not take any blood-thinning medications.
My roommate feels completely fine, and the dorm heating system is operating normally.
No, I do not have cancer, HIV, or any problem with my immune system.
No, I have never had a concussion or any head trauma prior to today.
I am really worried that I might have a concussion or even bleeding inside my skull.
I'm very anxious about whether I can practice and play in our upcoming basketball tournament.
I was hoping to get a head CT scan to make sure everything is okay inside, and to get advice on when I can play again.
I do not have any chronic medical illnesses.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription drugs, over-the-counter medicines, or dietary supplements.
I have no known allergies to medicines or anything else.
I do not smoke cigarettes or use e-cigarettes.
I only drink one or two beers socially on weekends, and I haven't had any alcohol today.
I am a college sophomore studying economics and living in an on-campus dormitory.
Both of my parents are healthy, and there is no family history of brain aneurysms or chronic headaches.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, oriented to person, place, and time with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, showing mild processing delay on complex tasks without confusion.
Focal mild contusion with localized tenderness over the right frontal-temporal scalp, with no laceration, step-off, or signs of basilar skull fracture.
No tenderness to palpation or percussion over the frontal or maxillary sinuses bilaterally.
Pupils are 3 mm, equal, round, and briskly reactive to light; visual fields are full, and fundoscopy demonstrates sharp optic disc margins without papilledema.
Tympanic membranes are intact and pearly gray bilaterally, with no hemotympanum, discharge, or retroauricular ecchymosis.
Cervical spine has no midline bony tenderness or palpable step-off, and active neck range of motion is fully preserved.
Neck is supple without nuchal rigidity; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are both negative.
Cranial nerves II through XII are intact with symmetric facial movements, normal extraocular motility, and normal sensation.
Muscle strength is 5/5 in all four extremities with normal muscle tone bilaterally.
Light touch and pinprick sensations are preserved and symmetric throughout all dermatomes.
Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, patellar, and Achilles tendons; plantar responses are flexor bilaterally.
Finger-to-nose testing is accurate, Romberg test is negative, and normal walking gait is steady with slight hesitation on tandem gait.
